title: Factcheck: How nuclear, gas, wind and solar power are affected during heatwaves - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon Brief rebuts the framing that heatwaves are mainly a wind-and-solar problem: during the record June–July 2026 European heat, thermal generation took the biggest hits — three of France's 57 reactors shut with output at another seven reduced (a ~9% dip), ~40% of south-east Europe's nuclear capacity (2.44GW) went offline on Danube drought, and gas plants lose ~13% capacity and 7% efficiency at 40C versus 20C. Solar set an EU record of 52TWh in June 2026 while UK balancing costs hit £1,400/MWh, making storage, interconnection and flexibility the actual binding constraint.

insights.claim: French daily electricity demand rose by almost 20% during a two-week heatwave in June 2026 as air conditioning and refrigeration load surged.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: A 20% demand step-change from a single weather event is the scale utilities must now plan for annually — bullish for peaking capacity, flexibility and cooling-linked load growth forecasts.
insights.quote: in France, daily electricity demand rose by almost 20% during a two-week heatwave in June 2026
insights.locator: For example, in France, daily electricity demand

insights.claim: Great Britain's system operator Neso paid as much as £1,400 per megawatt-hour to secure around 1.7GW of imported power on 24 June 2026, nearly 20 times the average June 2025 electricity price, citing extreme temperatures and low wind.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: 20x price multiples on balancing actions are the direct P&L upside for interconnector owners, battery operators and flexible demand — and the cost that lands in consumer bills.
insights.quote: paying as much as £1,400 a megawatt-hour to secure around 1.7 gigawatts (GW) of imported power, nearly 20 times the average price for electricity in June 2025
insights.locator: On Wednesday 24 June, for example

insights.claim: The sharpest price spikes during heatwaves occur in the early evening when solar output falls away but cooling demand persists and gas must ramp, an effect worsened by high international gas prices.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: The tradable window is the evening ramp, not midday — assets that can shift energy into the 5–9pm block capture the scarcity rent.
insights.quote: In the early evening hours, when gas power typically ramps up to replace solar, we have seen prices spike to extreme levels, made worse by high international gas prices.
insights.locator: Problems arise when the sun goes down

insights.claim: Extreme price spikes during heatwaves are best read as a market signal for flexibility — battery storage, demand response or increased interconnection — rather than as evidence of a generation-mix failure.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Frames heatwave volatility as a revenue opportunity for flexibility assets; policy response will likely subsidise or mandate the same assets.
insights.quote: The extreme price spikes that we witness during heatwaves are a blaring signal for more power system flexibility.
insights.locator: Dr Rosslowe says: The extreme price spikes

insights.claim: During the July 2026 heatwave three of France's 57 nuclear reactors had to shut down and generation was reduced at another seven, causing an almost 9% dip in power production.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: A near-10% output hit in the country supplying ~70% of its power from nuclear tightens the whole north-west European power balance during peak-price weeks.
insights.quote: During the July 2026 heatwave, three of France’s 57 nuclear reactors had to shut down. Generation was reduced at another seven, causing an almost 9% dip in power production.
insights.locator: During the July 2026 heatwave

insights.claim: On Monday 3 August 2026, around 2.44GW or 40% of south-east Europe's nuclear capacity was offline due to drought in the Danube, according to data company Montel.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Losing 40% of a region's nuclear fleet to hydrology is a security-of-supply event, not a rounding error — watch south-east European power forwards and emergency import flows.
insights.quote: on Monday 3 August, around 2.44GW or 40% of south-east Europe’s nuclear capacity was offline due to drought in the Danube
insights.locator: According to data company Montel

insights.claim: Only nuclear plants using once-through river cooling are severely exposed to heat and drought — about 60 of the world's 440 reactors, or 14% of the global fleet, of which eight are in France.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: A precise screen for climate-risk exposure in nuclear assets: cooling architecture, not geography, determines vulnerability — most of the global fleet is not at risk.
insights.quote: Around 60 of the world’s 440 reactors use once-through river cooling, of which eight are in France.
insights.locator: It is nuclear plants using river water

insights.claim: The binding constraint on reactors during heatwaves is usually legal rather than technical: thermal-discharge limits protecting aquatic life force curtailment, while even an extreme 15C rise in cooling-water temperature would cost a large reactor only about 6% of output.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Because the limit is regulatory, it can be waived — outage risk is a policy variable that governments can and do relax, which caps the downside for nuclear operators.
insights.quote: The real pressure point during a heatwave is usually legal rather than technical.
insights.locator: Michael Tadrous, a researcher at McMaster

insights.claim: Reactor shutdowns on high river temperatures are typically an automatic regulatory compliance response to protect local ecosystems rather than a technological fault, and in some extreme heatwaves those regulations are waived.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Headlines reading reactor shutdowns as nuclear unreliability misprice the asset; the mechanism is an environmental permit, not equipment failure.
insights.quote: typically an automatic response to comply with regulations to protect local ecosystems, rather than a technological fault
insights.locator: Henry Preston, a spokesperson for the industry body

insights.claim: Low river levels from drought have a far more prolonged impact on nuclear plant operations than elevated water temperatures, because temperatures recover quickly once a heatwave passes while water levels can stay depressed for weeks.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Duration risk sits with drought, not heat — hydrological forecasts are the better leading indicator for multi-week nuclear outages and regional power spreads.
insights.quote: low river levels can persist for much longer, if drought conditions continue. As a result, low water levels may have a more prolonged impact on plant operations than elevated water temperatures.
insights.locator: Preston tells Carbon Brief: In contrast to high river temperatures

insights.claim: Heatwaves cut annual nuclear generation by only 0.6% on average between 2003 and 2022, and across that whole period the only national fleet to lose more than 1% of annual output to heat- and drought-related curtailment was France in 2003, at 1.3%.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Annualised heat losses are immaterial to nuclear revenue models even as headline daily outages look dramatic — a gap between narrative and cash flow.
insights.quote: On average, heatwaves cut annual nuclear generation by 0.6% between 2003 and 2022
insights.locator: While heatwaves and drought can produce significant

insights.claim: France's river-cooled fleet lost 5.5TWh of output to the 2003 heatwave but only 0.5TWh in 2022 despite it being one of the most severe heat-and-drought summers on record — a roughly 90% reduction achieved through cooling upgrades, refined operating practices and maintenance scheduled around extreme heat.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Demonstrated 90% adaptation gains show climate-resilience capex in thermal fleets actually works, which supports the case for funding cooling retrofits over premature closures.
insights.quote: By 2022, one of the most severe heat-and-drought summers on record, losses had fallen to 0.5TWh, a reduction of roughly 90%, as utilities upgraded cooling systems, refined operating practices and scheduled maintenance around periods of
insights.locator: Tadrous says the nuclear power industry is already adapting

insights.claim: Concentration risk, not efficiency loss, is nuclear's real heatwave exposure: Romania's single plant at Cernavodă supplies 20% of national electricity, so Danube low water becomes an acute national energy-security problem.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Single-asset dependence turns a weather event into sovereign import exposure — screen national grids by largest-unit share when pricing climate risk.
insights.quote: Romania’s only nuclear power plant, at Cernavodă, is responsible for 20% of the nation’s electricity generation.
insights.locator: For example, Romania’s only nuclear power plant

insights.claim: French operator EDF is examining additional cooling towers for the sites most exposed to a warming climate, signalling a capex response to recurring heat curtailment.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: A concrete adaptation capex line for Europe's largest nuclear operator — order flow for cooling-tower and heat-exchange suppliers.
insights.locator: For example, French nuclear-plant operator EDF

insights.claim: The remaining obstacle to climate-proofing nuclear and its surrounding electricity systems is described as less about technical feasibility than about economic prioritisation and timely implementation.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Adaptation is a capital-allocation and permitting question, so the bottleneck is political will and tariffs, not technology risk.
insights.quote: less about “technical feasibility than of economic prioritisation and timely implementation”
insights.locator: There remain challenges for adapting nuclear power

themes.theme: Gas is not firm in a heatwave

insights.claim: At 40C a gas-fired power station can expect its capacity to fall by 13% and its efficiency by 7% compared with running at 20C, according to Electric Insights.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Derating dispatchable capacity by ~13% exactly when demand peaks means published gas capacity overstates real peak availability — a systematic error in adequacy assessments.
insights.quote: At 40C, a gas-fired power station can expect its capacity to be reduced by 13% and its efficiency by 7% compared to when running at 20C
insights.locator: As a matter of physics, the efficiency of gas power plants

insights.claim: Simple gas turbines — the peaking units relied on for rapid response — lose about 10% of power output per 10C of temperature rise, a harder hit than solar suffers.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: The very assets sold as heat-wave insurance degrade fastest in heat; peaker capacity-market valuations should be haircut for temperature.
insights.quote: Simple gas turbines (the kind which turn on rapidly to meet peak demand) are hit harder [than solar, for example], with their power output falling by about 10% per 10C.
insights.locator: Dr Iain Staffell, associate professor

insights.claim: Hot air's lower density means combined-cycle gas turbines get less oxygen mass per unit volume for combustion, physically limiting how much electricity they can generate when air temperatures are high.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: The gas derate is thermodynamic and unfixable by maintenance, so it will recur every heatwave regardless of plant age or operator quality.
insights.quote: hot air has a lower density than cool air. As gas CCGTs rely on burning a mix of gas and air, this lower density means air takes up more space, leaving less room for gas.
insights.locator: Additionally, as the UCS article notes

insights.claim: Gas plants accounted for around 79% of the capacity that dropped off the California system on 14 August 2020 during rolling blackouts, and a similar share the following day.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: The canonical US heatwave blackout was overwhelmingly a thermal-fleet failure, which undercuts the standard renewables-blamed post-mortem narrative.
insights.quote: gas plants made up around 79% of the capacity that dropped off the system on 14 August
insights.locator: While a number of factors contributed to the blackouts

insights.claim: Gas appears reliable in the UK mainly because only around 40% of the gas fleet runs at any one time, leaving spare units to call on — reliability is a function of surplus fleet, not of individual plant robustness.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: As the gas fleet shrinks with decarbonisation, this hidden reserve margin disappears and the reliability premium of gas erodes structurally.
insights.quote: on average, only around 40% of the gas fleet is in use at any one time
insights.locator: Whereas wind and solar are usually used

insights.claim: The heatwave problem with gas is priced, not physical: extra units can be persuaded to run, but only at prices described as paying through the nose at critical times, adding to already high energy bills.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Heat stress converts into consumer bills and generator margin rather than into lost load — the trade is in scarcity pricing, not blackouts.
insights.quote: The issue is less that they can’t deliver, but we have to pay through the nose to persuade more to turn on at critical times, adding to sky-high energy bills.
insights.locator: He adds: The issue is less that they can’t deliver

insights.claim: Transmission infrastructure degrades faster than generation in high heat, with power line capacity falling by up to 16% for a 10C temperature rise according to a report for the UK government.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Grid capacity, not generation, is the tightest link in a heatwave — supports capex and returns for transmission owners and reconductoring suppliers.
insights.quote: Power line capacity can fall by up to 16% for a 10C rise in temperature
insights.locator: He adds that the transmission system struggles more

insights.claim: High temperatures are linked to low wind speeds across three-quarters of the globe in data from 1980 to 2023, with wind power decreasing by an average of 30-50% during heatwaves across Australia, northern Asia and Europe.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: A 30-50% heat-correlated wind derate is a quantified capacity-credit input for any wind-heavy system's adequacy modelling and for merchant wind revenue forecasts.
insights.quote: across Australia, northern Asia and Europe, wind power decreased by an average of 30-50% during heatwaves
insights.locator: The study found that, as a result

insights.claim: The heat-wind relationship is not global: the Amazon, the North American Great Plains and central Africa actually see a slight increase in wind during high temperatures.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: US Great Plains wind assets do not carry the European heat-correlation penalty — a geographic differentiator when comparing wind portfolios.
insights.quote: with the Amazon, the Great Plains in North America and central Africa actually seeing a slight increase in wind during high temperatures
insights.locator: This is inconsistent globally, however

insights.claim: Heat domes hit wind output twice over — sustained high pressure suppresses wind speeds while hotter, less dense air carries less energy per unit volume.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Two compounding physical channels mean wind shortfalls in heatwaves are deeper than a simple wind-speed model implies.
insights.quote: Air is also less dense the hotter it is, so it carries less energy within it, so there is a double impact on wind turbines.
insights.locator: The very hottest days tend to create heat domes

insights.claim: UK wind generation fell to around 15% of the electricity mix in June 2026 against a monthly average of about 30%, halving its contribution just as record temperatures pushed demand up.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: A concrete magnitude for the summer wind gap in Britain, which is exactly the shortfall that interconnectors and batteries were paid extreme prices to fill.
insights.quote: wind generation fell to around 15% of the electricity mix due to low wind speeds, from an average for the month of about 30%
insights.locator: In the UK in June 2026, wind generation fell

insights.claim: System operators do not treat summer wind shortfalls as a concern because wind follows well-established seasonal patterns already planned for and is complementary to solar, with still but clear heatwave conditions favouring one when they penalise the other.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Portfolio-level thinking, not per-technology availability, is the correct lens for renewables reliability — and the reason wind remains classed as heatwave-resilient by the UK government.
insights.quote: Heatwaves often bring still, but clear conditions, highlighting the benefit of wind and solar as a duo – poor conditions for one often mean good conditions for the other.
insights.locator: Dr Chris Rosslowe, senior energy analyst

insights.claim: Media attribution of grid strain to renewables is demonstrably selective: the Daily Mail blamed wind for UK grid strain on 24 June 2026 while its own article acknowledged gas plants had been forced to cut output by 2.5GW that day.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Public narrative on heatwave grid stress is systematically biased against renewables, which distorts political risk and policy expectations relative to the physical data.
insights.quote: this did not stop the anti-renewables Daily Mail from attempting to blame the technology for strain on the UK grid on 24 June 2026, despite its own article acknowledging that gas plants had also been forced to cut their output by 2.5GW on
insights.locator: However, this did not stop the anti-renewables

insights.claim: Solar cell efficiency losses to heat are modest and well characterised — around 0.4-0.5% of output per 1C of temperature rise, or 0.2-0.5% per degree above 25C in a UK government evidence review — and are easily outweighed by the extra sunlight hours during hot spells.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Quantifies why the solar-struggles-in-heat claim is wrong by an order of magnitude versus the irradiance gain, supporting solar yield assumptions in hot markets.
insights.quote: Each 1C of temperature rise reduces output by around 0.4-0.5%, according to a recent study.
insights.locator: While hot weather does reduce the efficiency of solar cells

insights.claim: Solar generated a record 52TWh across the EU in June 2026, beating the record of 47TWh set only the month before.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Back-to-back monthly records show EU solar output compounding fast enough to reshape summer midday power prices and gas burn.
insights.quote: Solar generated a record 52TWh across the EU in June 2026, beating the high set just the month before of 47TWh.
insights.locator: Similar generation highs were seen across Europe

insights.claim: Across a four-day UK heatwave in June 2026 solar generated 484GWh, a 46% increase over the same period a week earlier.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Solar output rises materially precisely when heat-driven demand peaks, making it a demand-correlated rather than merely intermittent resource.
insights.quote: solar generated 484 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of electricity – a 46% increase over the same period a week earlier
insights.locator: For example, across a four-day heatwave in the UK

insights.claim: Solar output and air-conditioning demand line up both seasonally and intraday, with Great Britain's solar surging to 13.9GW mid-afternoon on 26 June 2026 as demand also peaked.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Correlation between solar generation and cooling load raises solar's effective capacity credit in hot markets — relevant to how AC-driven load growth should be resourced.
insights.locator: For example, on the hottest day of the year

insights.claim: Across June 2026 homes with solar panels generated the equivalent of five hours of free self-supplied air conditioning, framing rooftop solar as a direct household cooling-cost hedge.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: A consumer-facing value proposition that supports residential solar-plus-storage demand as AC penetration rises in Europe.
insights.quote: homes with solar panels generated the equivalent of five hours of “free” self-supplied air conditioning
insights.locator: Across June 2026, homes with solar panels

insights.claim: Solar suppresses power prices during daylight hours but leaves an unresolved challenge in managing the evening solar decline, which coincides with the usual evening demand increase.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: The duck-curve evening ramp is where the value migrates as solar builds — the structural case for four-hour-plus storage and flexible demand.
insights.locator: Indeed, as Dr Rosslowe tells Carbon Brief

themes.theme: Storage as the swing solution and its limits

insights.claim: More than 108GW of battery storage was added globally in 2025 alone according to the International Energy Agency, making batteries the dominant energy-storage technology.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: A 108GW annual run-rate anchors demand forecasts for cells, BESS integrators and the lithium/LFP supply chain feeding them.
insights.quote: with more than 108GW of battery storage added in 2025 alone, according to the International Energy Agency
insights.locator: The category of technologies is dominated by batteries

insights.claim: Battery performance degrades once temperatures exceed optimal levels and high heat accelerates degradation of lithium-ion components, so storage is not immune to the conditions it is deployed to manage.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Warranty and degradation assumptions in hot-climate BESS projects deserve scrutiny; thermal management is a differentiator between suppliers.
insights.locator: However, batteries are not without their challenges

insights.claim: UK government analysis found prolonged very high temperatures could in theory overwhelm batteries' built-in cooling and pose thermal runaway and explosion risks, but noted those cooling systems are routinely designed to handle temperatures up to 45C.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: The 45C design threshold is the number to test against local climate projections when underwriting BESS safety and insurance risk.
insights.quote: posing risks such as thermal runaway and explosions
insights.locator: Analysis for the UK government found

insights.claim: Australia's 4.3GW of large-scale battery capacity plus pumped hydro was tested in its most severe heatwave in years at the start of 2026, with output and operating times reduced by the increased need to run cooling systems above 40C.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Parasitic cooling load cuts deliverable storage output in extreme heat — a real-world derate to build into hot-market revenue models.
insights.locator: Australia – which now has 4.3GW

insights.claim: Pumped hydro storage can be significantly impacted by drought, making the leading long-duration storage technology vulnerable to the same hydrological stress that curtails river-cooled nuclear.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Drought is a correlated risk across nuclear and pumped hydro simultaneously — a hidden concentration in water-dependent portfolios.
insights.locator: Other storage technologies also face challenges

insights.claim: A combination of solar and battery energy storage kept the lights on in California during a 2024 heatwave, demonstrating that day-charged storage discharged into evening peaks can prevent the generation constraints that caused earlier blackouts.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: California is the working proof-of-concept for solar-plus-storage as heatwave insurance, a template other hot grids will follow.
insights.quote: a combination of solar and battery energy storage “kept the lights on” in California amid a heatwave in 2024
insights.locator: Despite these challenges, the use of battery storage

insights.claim: Battery storage, interconnection, demand flexibility and dynamic tariffs should become a core part of grid planning and power market design because heatwaves will only get more severe.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Names the four policy-favoured flexibility categories likely to attract regulatory support and capital as heat events recur.
insights.quote: Heatwaves will not go away – they will only get more severe in the future.
insights.locator: In a statement, Pawel Czyzak

insights.claim: All electricity generation types are affected by extreme heat, yet commentators are quick to blame intermittent wind and solar while downplaying the impact on gas and nuclear — a systematic asymmetry in public discussion.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Where public narrative diverges from physical performance data, policy and asset valuations can misprice — the gap itself is the opportunity.
insights.quote: some commentators are quick to point the finger at “intermittent” wind and solar, while downplaying the impact on sources such as gas or nuclear power
insights.locator: Yet, while all types of electricity generation

insights.claim: France has seen heatwave-driven reductions in nuclear generation in 2003, 2006, 2015, 2018, 2019, 2022 and 2025, making the 2026 curtailments a recurring and forecastable phenomenon rather than a novel shock.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Seven prior episodes in two decades means summer French nuclear derates should already be in forward curves — surprise is only in the magnitude.
insights.quote: France has seen reductions in nuclear generation due to heatwaves in 2003, 2006, 2015, 2018, 2019, 2022 and 2025
insights.locator: (This is a well-known phenomenon

insights.claim: Around 12% of the French nuclear fleet was offline on Monday 3 August 2026 for heat-related reasons, though that was expected to drop to 7% by Tuesday, showing how quickly heat-driven outages reverse.
insights.speaker: Molly Lempriere
insights.so_what: Fast mean-reversion in heat outages means the associated price spikes are short-dated — favouring flexible assets over structural capacity additions.
insights.quote: as much as 12% of the French nuclear fleet was offline due to heat-related reasons, although that had been expected to drop to 7% by Tuesday
